en: Preface to the *Guanhe ji* (Anthology on Contemplating the River):
Long ago, a Brahmin left the household life; when he returned with his hair already white, a neighbor saw him and asked, "Is that former man still here?
The Brahmin replied, "I am the same person as before, yet I am not the person of before. I have often savored these words and felt sorrow for them. As for me—
Forty years have passed since my birth. When I reflect upon myself this year, I am not the same as I was in previous years;
when I reflect upon myself today, I am not the same as I was yesterday. Like wood and fire, there is no cessation; every thought-moment (citta-kṣaṇa) undergoes transition and decay.
If one seeks that which constitutes "self," it cannot be found. With this unfindable self, [one should] hew...
They grasp at these things and rely upon them as being real; thus, likes and dislikes, hatred and love, become entangled and chaotic, perishing along with life itself.
This is truly something that should cause one to feel deep pain and wring one’s hands in distress. Nevertheless, this merely describes their state of transformation.
If one knows that such things cannot be attained and never relies upon them as being real, then even their transformations—
This is precisely that which is unchanging. To know that the changing is unchanging, even ten thousand deaths and ten thousand births are equal to a single moment without distinction;
how much more so in the span of forty years? I was eighteen years old.
He first began composing poetry. Over more than twenty years, as his works accumulated, he compiled them into two collections.

One is titled the *Ceshai Ji* (Collection for Measuring the Sea), which exclusively records poems on the sacred virtues of successive reigns, as well as various verses in praise of worthy men. The other is titled the *Guanghe Ji* (Collection for Viewing the River);

these are generally compositions that evoke emotion through the observation of objects, expressing long-standing reflections in rhythmic verse. Among them are accounts of the unions and separations of natural kinship, and the vicissitudes of human affairs.
[This] is concluded. That the Way and its arts follow the *wei* (leather) [robe] can be fully examined and known therein.

When the Buddha was at the Jetavana Monastery, he preached the Dharma for King Prasenajit. He asked: "Do you now observe this Ganges River? Compare it with the vision of the river you had when you were a child."
"Is there childhood and old age? He replied, "No. The Buddha said, "That which changes undergoes extinction. That which does not change is fundamentally without birth or death.
How could birth and death be experienced within it? Moreover, why limit this to childhood and old age alone?
By this same principle, whether it be a hundred years, a thousand years, one kalpa, ten kalpas, or even immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the nature of phenomena remains unchanging."
Transmigration: neither as a child nor as an old man, without departing from the present thought, one directly realizes Bodhi.
As for the composition of this poem, there is no author, yet there is no absence of an author. Such is its contemplation; it is simply this.
The Master, by the river, said: "That which passes away is like this; it flows on without ceasing, day and night. Its contemplation, too, is simply this. Qianlong 4.
The fourteenth year. On the full moon of the third lunar month, Peng Shengshao inscribed this.
*Guanhé jí jiéchāo* (Annotated Excerpts from the Collection on Observing the River), authored by Zhīguīzǐ Peng Jìqīng; excerpted by his private disciple [Name].
When the list of those who passed the metropolitan examination was issued, I secured a place among the successful; yet, feigning illness, I did not attend the palace examination.

The cassia tree harbors its extraordinary brilliance; enduring the cold, it is somewhat self-satisfied. It offers its sincere thanks to the eastern wind, yet the wind blows without causing it to bear fruit.

Gathering the ancient spirit, I have plucked the spring from the riverbank. Transplanted before the hall, the tree’s withered and flourishing states are difficult to distinguish; by whose hand was this single breath forged?
At Gao Bridge, I recall Liang Boluan.

Having completed the "Five Sighs" (Wuyi) Rhapsody, he departs from the capital; far longing for the spirit of Lord Yanling, he heads toward the coastal frontier. His sense of duty toward sovereign and subject is thin, yet his heart still turns to friendship;
carrying his wife and children, he has no home left behind. His unrestrained sentiments have long followed the cold current, and the lingering rays of the setting sun still cling to the wild fields.
Setting out at an oblique angle, I could not bear to seek the market of Meiwei again. Where in the red dust can one lie amidst the mists and clouds?
When Wang Dashen sent me a poem discussing our studies, I immediately composed a sequel (Recording One):
Wangzi’s friendships are simple; he comes and goes as the mood moves him. His detached disposition seems devoid of emotion, yet his profound intent is manifest in the mutual nourishment we share.
The spring breeze opens the door; tomorrow the sun shall shine upon your boat. With what intent do you ask whether I stay or go?
With a gentle smile, he breaks into a lofty song. *Ten Poems on the Impulse to Travel North, No.
3:* This body has neither departure nor dwelling; north and south are both my home. As for the parting wine, let others urge me to drink; though at the edge of the world, I feel no sense of distance.
Lakes and mountains lend themselves to solitary chanting; wind and rain enter the withered raft. Sitting here, my poetic inspiration is stirred; flowers bloom everywhere upon the empty sands.
Pointing toward the path of the Qing River, I find myself once again in accord with the Sage’s heart. Where white clouds have no end, the emerald waters are all at once deep.

The flavors left behind transcend both the open and the blocked; forgetting words, one cuts off the ways of the ancients. A long song vibrates through the forest thickets; among woodcutters and herdsmen, there are those who share this same resonance.

Gazing afar at the slender, bright moon, deep within the inner chambers, this night draws to a close. Idly holding an ancient Buddhist verse, I practice frugality like the meal of a decaying Confucian scholar.
The autumn waters pity my lingering sorrows; the plum blossoms share the cold with you. Lumen is not far away; its wondrous essence lies in the peace of a single branch.
One of Four Miscellaneous Verses Written at My Lodging in Rehe:

In this low-roofed house with mud walls, the courtyard is vast and open. I cherish our conversations over volumes of poetry, gathered in joyful intimacy. Before the gate, carriages and horses pass by in a bustling rush.
Past. All day long, the green mountains look on with smiles.

In response to the Grand Scholar’s letter regarding the flourishing of the Apricot Terrace (the site of Confucius), which has long since fallen into decay: amidst a heap of hearsay and superficial learning, one merely deceives oneself in vain. Only by chance have I encountered the thread [of the Dharma] at Vulture Peak.
The Way: Opening Heaven with a single stroke, it is utterly without beginning.
Regarding the "Song of Imprisonment" (Jiyoucao), Han Yu composed an imitation of it;
its words abound in expressions of sorrow and suffering, yet they do not fully capture the inner intent of the *Yi* (Book of Changes).
In his observation of this, he distinguished it by proposing:
"The sun is deep and solemn, yet its movement never ceases; the sun is profound and mysterious, yet its brilliance never falters. He reveres the early morning and the night."
Fuxi was the one who established the processes; it is simply that there is no "acting. There is neither deficiency nor completion. Alas! This culture resides herein;
what more need I strive for?
The second of "Five Poems on What I Contemplate."
That which my mind dwells upon is the Terrace of Apricots. There is a pheasant in the beam and orchids in the valley.

To encompass the four seas, one need have no active striving; to dwell in poverty, one drinks water and finds joy. Joy upon joy—who shares this heart? I stroke the *zeng* lute and play the *Yan* zither.
Tracing back the ancient ford, I find it level for all eternity. Mountain flowers bloom as the mountain sun reaches noon.

That which I contemplate dwells in Longchang; my steadfast will gives rise to the light of Heaven. I unroll ancient scrolls and penetrate the vast void; I look up at the soaring kites and gaze down at the joyful fish.
The spring breeze shines as a multitude of sages assemble; the clanging of sentry-drums falls silent as the sound of stringed songs resounds.
I pay homage to General Ma Yuan, and our dream of continuity is renewed; I remember my old mountain, where the grasses are newly green.
At Bilin Station, parting with Luo Taishan:
The river moon shines as you depart; The river wind blows me back home. In this lightness, we have become far apart; With a smile, I trust in the workings of Heaven.
Awakening from the turbidity, I gaze long at my sword; our profound pact is to close the door together. In this place of silent spiritual communion, do not inquire whether it is right or wrong.
Parting Song for Dai-shen’s Departure for Lan’an and His Appointment as Principal of Jianyang Academy (Record One):
The spring breeze passes over the river; the grass grows green along the banks of Chū. You travel the road of a thousand li; our parting falls upon this very hour.
This moment shall not be found again; who else shall be my companion in the Way? I pour wine and offer these words to you: may your virtue be renewed daily.
When the time comes that the zither-playing has ceased, may you and your disciples harmonize with the true nature of Heaven.
In response to the gift of Cao Lukai, following his rhyme:

Beyond the mundane world, our hearts find true affinity; Relying on each other in the cassia hall, we are severed from clamor and dust. Carrying zithers to enter the sea is a promise for future years;
Binding oneself to the mountains with wax-soled boots is a cause not yet finished. When clouds clear, the moon appears in the empty pool; As snow melts, the plum buds already bloom.
Spring has arrived. This evening in the southern garden, I am weary of your constant remembrance; I sigh deeply as the years of my life renew themselves once more.

On the occasion of Master Shen Lifu’s seventieth birthday, I sought refuge from guests in a monk’s quarters; the following day, you paid me a visit, and I have received this poem which I offer to you in tribute.

The Master is willing to shoulder the era of Great Peace; yet in his declining years, he still cherishes the beauty of the world for himself. Happening to hear the sound of the bell, he takes up his staff and departs;

leisurely, he watches the shadows of flowers pass slowly across the courtyard. When the mind returns to its original source, there are a thousand poems; though worldly affairs remain, there is but a single cup of wine.
My desolate cottage is troubled by inquiries after my health; here, our true intentions are known to one another.
Sitting at night, I record my thoughts and send them to the three brothers of the Xue family.

Time has passed without my being aware of it; there has been not a single word in exchange through our poetic exchanges. The moon over the water finds its companion in stillness; the birds in the forest find their own delight in tranquility.

With an impartial mind, observe the illusory transformations; extinguish consciousness to find the path home. Do not shed the tears of Yang Zhu; the long days pass away in vain. [In this] Preface to the Draft of Mr.
Shen Lifu’s *Thirty-Six Flowers*, Yuanming loved chrysanthemums and Liangxi loved lotuses.
Though lotuses and chrysanthemums have their seasons, who can compare them to one who contemplates them throughout the year? Yet none surpasses this Master.
Flowers bloom upon the field of the mind; turn left, turn right. The scenery is resplendent—neither winter nor spring. Here are fish and hawks alike;
Yan Hui lives in the alley, and Confucius dwells by the river. He beckons me to follow him, to gaze at the flowers as they reach their peak.
On the fifth day of the second month in the Gengyin year, Wang Xiangshan invited me, along with several friends from Mudu, to visit Mount Hua and ascend Lotus Peak. Four Poems.
For years I have kept my door closed, neglecting this fine Mount Hua. Since you, my friend, could love it as well, my companions likewise found leisure.
Meeting a monk as if an old acquaintance, he leans against a tree and breaks into a smile. He ascends directly toward the high peak; who knows the hardships of the bird-path?
(The stone wall bears the two characters "bird-path").
The lotus flowers never fall; the waters of the pond have long been deep. Only this traveler amidst the dust speaks of seeking within a dream.
White clouds open the ancient path; the setting sun lodges my heart’s longing for home. I recall the Master Xikong once more—his pure breeze reaches us even today.
(Zhu Baimin, in his later years, lived beneath Lotus Flower Peak, where he cultivated the Pure Land practice and styled himself the Layman Xikong.)

The old man of Yushan has endured hardship; his kasaya is entrusted to his twilight years. Among humans and devas, he is like a withered tree leaf; his loyalty and filial piety are the incense smoke from an ancient furnace.

Seeking the Dharma-milk of Linji, he drinks the azure spring from an empty mind. His friends pity Zi Jun—who, having first been a dharma-brother to Yushan, later gave his life for Nanjing—and put him to the test before the wind of the white blade.

(Xiong Yushan left the household life during the chaos and received the Dharma from Master Jiqui; he resided at Huashan and drank from the Azure Spring. Jin Zi Jun was initially a dharma friend of Yushan, but later sacrificed his life for Nanjing.)

The affairs of a thousand autumns are not yet exhausted; the lakes and mountains stretch to the very horizon. Cherries and flowers are but the dreams of ants; the winds atop the trees are the strife of the giants.
Barefoot, I tread upon precarious rocks; my solitary staff hangs against the azure sky. Seeking a place to go below, I point out the red of fallen blossoms.
Inscription on Ding Yunpeng’s Painting of Arhats:
"The Sun Rises to Illuminate All Beings. Birth and death have no time of rest; within the vast ocean of desire, all deluded children are intoxicated with their own bones."
How pitiable is this wondrously luminous mind! It remains thus forever through the ages. Having withdrawn the body to escape the burning house, who among the six thieves can deceive it?

At the Twin Trees, receiving the Buddha’s command, he dwells for a long time on the divine mountain. He has cut off the boundaries of coming and going; in his subtlety and silence, there is no interval between existence and non-existence.
The painter captures the ultimate truth; a pure breeze washes the youthful countenance. Sentient beings await his benefit as he shakes his mendicant’s staff and wanders through the human world.
Inscription on a Painting of a Fisherman:
Worldly wisdom grows ever more urgent by the day, yet the lives of creatures remain miserable and unrelieved. Alas! The rivers and seas are vast—yet who can provide shelter for even a single fish?
This man alone harbors a vast ambition; with hands folded in his sleeves, he dwells within a boat. He sings aloud "Return Home" (*Guqulai*), and I perceive that his intent knows nothing more.

Entering Dengwei to view the withered plum blossoms—blossoms that wish to fall yet do not fully fall—he led me into the mountains to the Mountain Pavilion. The flowers bloom like gathering clouds and scatter like dispersing mist.
Smoke. It flutters at the mountain peak and is cast down at the foot of the hill. Is it fragrance? Is it not fragrance? Is it form? Is it not form?
Who can attain the pervasive presence of form and fragrance? Ascending the mountain, descending the mountain, the sun declines. The spring breeze sends me back and forth.
Inscription on the "Bathing the Whales" and "Celebrating Family Prosperity" Paintings One might think the body has been cast away;
with autumn winds suddenly blowing far off, The spring colors of the previous year are beautiful; suddenly one returns to one's old garden.
The wine is ready; I first open the jar. Fragrant flowers scent the quiet closed door. Who would have known the nobility of bells and tripods? For now, let me try on the "Old Lai" robe.
Traveling north, I encounter these matters; ancient walls display painted figures. A grass bridge within a single dream—sentient beings form this world, silent as they face the west wind.
Falling powder leaves the delicate maidservant withered; wandering silken threads entangle the young page. Young travelers from the Five Tombs—do not hasten here!
Before the courtyard lies scattered grain, where birds and sparrows alike rejoice. But when they turn their heads and see a human figure, they suddenly fly back into the distant clouds.
When the mind of spontaneity is fully realized, one may join the multitude of all things. Amidst the spring breeze wherever one goes, who would not share in this with you?
Passing by Qinxi An, I recall Master Xiaofeng;
returning from visiting a friend ten li away in the western suburbs, I linger awhile by Huayang Bridge. Beneath the shade of pines, a single path leads to a gate that remains ever closed.
Closed. Yet, for the sake of the idle person, he opens it specifically.
Coming and going, how could one find ease of mind? After Zhaozhou’s tea is finished, his intent is serene. Returning, he adds a new daily practice:
burning incense until it is spent, facing the moon in silent contemplation.

Ten Poems Written on the Way North, Expressing My Feelings News from the Jade Pond announces the arrival of early spring; I am utterly grieved for the aged minister of Mount Xiangshan. Cane in hand, I again seek a ferry at the river’s edge;
Is there no kind word to comfort these nights and mornings?
In a life of detachment, cherish the lengthening days; let the sutras follow you and be companions to the incense in the burner. The Buddha-dharma of the Pang family is not much:
it is simply speaking of the roundness of the waters of this one realm.
Stalled in the middle of Piesha Lake on my long journey, The wind is ravenous and the snow is cruel, as waves repeatedly startle me. A string of prayer beads has followed him away;
I shall not ask about life or death along the way.
The wheels and hooves of the world’s chariots have scarcely ceased their toil from south to north. My gaze reaches to the setting sun at an ancient ford;
the boundless tears of heroes have long since been spent, yet the Yellow River flows on as ever toward the east.
Amidst the stable’s horses, the sound of the alarm bells rings out; as ever, the lotus-water clock marks the purity of the six periods.
Like a crescent moon hanging upon the eastern wall, it illuminates me as I remain sleepless until the fifth watch.
By the walls of Yishui City, green trees cast their shade; here in years past, my friend spread his robe. The eastern wind has blown away the warbling of the yellow orioles;
how melancholy that the grass before the hall grows deep once more. (Xue Jia Sanzeng presided over the Yizhou Academy.)

By the roadside, songs of praise recognize the lingering thoughts of his departure; the wilds are no longer wasteland or barren, and all things are free from blemish. The wind and moon of the Southern Garden are as they were before;
yet the mountain mounds fall into decay once more at this very hour—[for my elder brother served in Xincheng and Wenshang, where he was effective in promoting water conservancy].

The footprints of the Mountain Man of the Five Peaks are vast and indistinct; he chants with the wind and plays with the moon, utterly wild and unrestrained. When the crane departs toward the heavens, he turns his head back once more;
at the end of the clear night, the West Lake reflects his shadow in cool serenity. (He once paid a visit to Master Sang Taofu at Luyuan Academy; having returned to Hangzhou, he passed away.
He traveled extensively across the Five Peaks and thus took that as his self-designation.)
Beneath Mount Chengfu lies a refined hermitage; Huì has repeatedly sent me letters on silk. Having realized how excellent are the verses of Ziyang, I wonder:
what are the tidings of the east wind like lately? (Chengfu was the place where Master Han returned to his studies.)
Snow and ice for my writing, stone huts for my poetry; Dipping my pen while dwelling in the mountains, I return from my dreams. With every note, the song enters the Chang'an Road;
How could there ever be a single strand of silk caught beneath one's feet? (I recited several of Shiwu’s poems while traveling in a carriage).
Crossing Liangxi, I recall the late Minister Gao Zhongxian:

Suddenly realizing where I belong, this life is fulfilled. Resting my arm and drinking water, I have forgotten all worldly attachments. The floating clouds do not alter the color of the green mountains;
I wander toward the riverbank to pay tribute to Qu Yuan.
A single phrase at the time of departure finds few who understand it. In the water pavilion, he once sat deeply in meditation. The spring breeze fills the courtyard, unable to be confined;
Flowers and fragrance remain in disarray even unto this day. (In his final letter to others, he wrote: "The mind is like the great void; fundamentally, there is neither birth nor death.")
At Mount Tai, bones accumulate like mountains and tears like oceans; how can one escape this entangling net of attachment? From now on, plant the seeds of the lotus;
as the moon traverses the vast sky, its reflection remains upon the waves.
Boundless spring colors fill the rustic gate; through kalpas past, the grace of rain and dew is hard to repay.
With a single incense stick in the burner and one invocation of the Buddha’s name, I pass the days and nights within the ocean-tide resonance.
Seeking spring within Gaomin Temple, I go; Coming to view the moon at Xiaoxiawan, I return. At every place, mountains and rivers are eternally in cessation;
The lotus blossoms beneath my feet for your sake.
With bundles of rushes, there was a covenant awaiting your return; with the *Avataṃsaka* to shield one's eyes, it is called "closing the gate.
Who would believe that within the pores of Samantabhadra, the wind and moon of Mount Ni have never been idle?
Inscription on My Cousin Baoyuan’s Painting of Plum Blossoms Amidst Deep Shadow The myriad things are harmonized by the primal transformation;
from this, the Great Mystery returns. In the empty mountains, vast and devoid of people, who beholds the cold blossoms bloom?
In the desolate midst of ice and snow, one occasionally hears the mournful cries of monkeys and birds.
My elder brother, the ancient sage, tastes like the rich flavor of *mishu* wine; he cannot be stained by the mundane world. We have met here as figures within a painting.
The flickering light of the breeze blows; who could fail to envy the springtime of the peach and plum?
Entering Panshan to visit Qianxiang Temple, I sought the secluded along winding paths.
To enjoy solitude alone satisfied my lifelong aspirations. Crossing the stone bridge at a leisurely pace, I quietly listened to the sound of flowing water.
Strange peaks evoke ancient sentiments; crimson leaves fall upon the shimmering waters. Pointing out the excellence of this monastery, I drift away from worldly passions.
Resting at Wansong Temple—looking afar toward Wansong Temple—I return to the thousand-fathom mountain. Above there is still a path; wherever I am, I shall steal a moment’s leisure.
All the myriad pipes are hushed at once; the traveler departs and does not return. In this desolate stillness, with whom can one converse? I personally knock upon the gates of the Purple Palace.
I bestow upon myself the silent spring of the primordial source, where my beard and brows are reflected, unstained by dust. According to my lot, I examine all things with vermilion and lead.

Transformation: By chance, singing and weeping occur within human relations; the moonlight at the edge of heaven is originally inexhaustible. How many times has the peach blossom by the cave mouth renewed itself?
Desiring to play a single melody upon Mount Penglai, amidst the vast expanse of clouds and waters, who else is there as a neighbor?
Seeing the new poem shown by Shen Lifu:
"Silence and speech are matters for a thousand autumns; the brilliance of its style fills the eye. The Master is truly at ease; few know our Way."

Delighting in this era of Great Peace, the spring days remain slow to pass. There is no need to keep one’s door closed for long; this intention is entirely free from self-interest. In response to Dashen’s discourse on learning:
The flow of the Yángjiāng never ceases; everywhere it connects to a single source. The jade moon hangs suspended in solitary radiance; the pivot of the stars turns within the vast emptiness of space.

One must ascend straight up the perilous cliff; an inch of steel will surely achieve its purpose. The events of a thousand autumns pass like shadows—what need is there to labor over their differences?
Inscribed as a Continuation to the *Xiyuan Yajiji* (Elegant Gathering at the Western Garden):

The elegance of past and present is an illusion of clouds and mist; A single scroll of ink and color, its intent is vast and remote. Within the dream of the Hu-die butterfly, who is the one [awakened]?
I dwell within the Peach Blossom Spring, unaware of the passing years. Rivers wind through secluded coves, lush and deep green; The moon shines upon my jade cup, ever full and round.
In the desolation of the river and sky after spring has gone, I shall let out a long, resonant sigh atop the verdant peaks.
Seeing Kang Zhonggeng Return to Taiyuan:
On this day you depart; mountain paths and waterways alike. People pity you at the Cold Food Festival; Guests have dispersed from the city of Helu.

In the fine rain, I long for our former seats; with this clear breeze, this life is sufficient. Within the lingering dreams of my official quarters, the shadows of paulownia trees fall as autumn sounds descend.
Entering the capital to visit my parents, I follow the rhyme of Li Yuding:
Within these shared hundred years, as you travel on, do not let your pace be in vain haste. The white flower is where I find my delight; I cherish you and think of you constantly.

Drinking water, one knows its taste or lack thereof; smelling incense, one knows whether it is known or not. My longing for home now has a place of rest; let us sing of the wind amidst the late spring.

Traveling north, I encounter these matters: my quiet gate is empty, with bamboo and trees; accustomed to rivers and bridges on distant roads, I have carried with me the moon of the Five Lakes, which thereby sheds its light over a thousand li.
Gathered in a circle, we are far from home; we share laughter and joy within these lofty halls. Incidentally, we speak of the discourse on non-arising; before the lamp, we raise a cup in toast.
Regretting our parting as autumn draws near, we pour wine at the crossroads. Though the greens have but one flavor, our lives have shared both fragrance and stench.
The mountain colors are purified by the frost; the river current flows level as it reaches the sea. On the road beside Laolao Pavilion, let not the traveler’s dream be startled.

The fire of the nature of history burns away all attachments; emptiness is truly pervasive throughout the great thousandfold world. Pity those caught in the illusory net, entangled in their own continuity. One morning, they are cast away in the red furnace.
Within, from amidst immeasurable light, white lotuses surge forth.
Accompanying Old Monk Xiangshan as he crossed Upper Sand, I presented this to Jiang Yuanbiao.
Leisurely attending to the old monk, we visited the mountain home. A single stream flows along, trailing the evening glow; flowers fall upon the empty courtyard, never once [stopping].
Sweeping the floor, I joyfully welcome the arrival of guests and brew fresh tea.
What shall become of this waning life drifting as a traveler? Turning my head, I see my old home by the Western Pond. With one hundred and eight beads of the prayer wheel, I pass the long days;
in every dust mote lies the Land of Ultimate Bliss, with nothing else remaining.
The two daughters, Ahuan and Aying, recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra*, and the "Universal Gate" Chapter (*Pumenpin*).
They were also each instructed to transcribe one copy of these texts. Three poems were composed: Curtains of bright pearls are slanted and rolled up;
incense smoke deepens within the seal-patterned burner. The *kalaviṅka* has shed its shell and utters its wondrous song. A single spoonful of ink flowing from the brush is a field of merit.
Water. Heavenly flowers fall like rain upon the shaded courtyard.
I offer long lamentation before the Compassionate Teacher; may my vows for the endless cycle of birth and death be boundless. From this moment, with a single thought, I know how to dedicate [merit];
from amidst the sword-trees, precious lotuses emerge.
What prevents a young maiden from manifesting an illusory body? Throughout the ten directions, all is pure and utterly free of dust. One hears this directly within the ocean-like tidal voice;
upon the willow branches, not a trace of spring remains.
My wife said to her two daughters: "If you wish to meet again for a long time, you must seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
Otherwise, within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, each will follow its own conditions; this is truly to be feared.
Her words were full of profound meaning, and I have composed a poem to record them.
The Buddha-mind is precisely the mind of sentient beings. A bird in the empty forest, a crane in the shade. I tell you this one phrase;
take it to heart: where the river of craving dries up, the jeweled pond is deep.

The dream has been shattered; years have passed by the river isles. Amidst the sound of drums and bells, I prostrate before the Golden Immortal. Together with him, we alternately play the melody of non-arising;
this is the separate transmission of the *Zhou-nan* outside the teachings.
In Response to Dashen (The Second of Four Poems):
The spirit of the "Great Dragon" of the lakes and seas remains magnificent. Having finished reciting the Golden Sutra, he turns again to the *Li Sao*.
It would be well to take the waters of ten-thousand-acre Xiangjiang River And plant there lotus flowers ten fathoms high.
The light from the white tuft of hair illuminates boundless lands; the cries of water birds proclaim the gate of non-duality.
With a single state of equanimity is true liberation; there is nothing further to discuss with you.
Two of the Ten Miscellaneous Recollections:
Writing on Reciting the Sutra a Hundred Times while Also Mindfully Reciting the Buddha’s Name. Though one’s faith may be good, how coarse one’s temperament is!
Without cause, one casts a cold eye upon others; Afterward, will one gain any power from Amitābha?
The Jiang family’s new work honors Xu and Zheng; Master Yu’s commentary on Su and Huang is for those with eye ailments. Toiling in hardship all year long, no one asks after him;
beneath the old tree in the empty courtyard, the evening sun sinks low.
I always find it vexing that you are so boastful and reckless. The achievements of the eras of Tang and Yu were merely ordinary matters.
The spring breeze by the banks of the Yi River is my family’s business; do not envy the silken cords of Guan Zhong and Shang Yang. (One of four poems presented to Liu Chongru)
The River Commissioner, Lord Yao, seeing that my humble poem resembled that of the late Lord Shi Du, composed two quatrains to be inscribed here.
The structure of the mountain hall at Pingzhi has been newly renovated;
a secluded path now leads through. For a time, I cast off my official robes and sit amidst the spring breeze. Carving the mountains and channeling the waters—truly a matter of leisure.
Matters of state—its governance and strategy—are pointed out before one’s eyes.
The Recluse of Huayang (the author’s own style name) possesses a noble bearing; in his later years, he has entrusted his livelihood to a single ladle.
Having finished his long-drawn sighs under the bright moon upon the river, who will share these pure verses with him on this cool night?
Four Verses on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* Written by Chan Master Languan The white tuft of light fills the vast void;
Ordinary beings and sages alike return to the midst of tranquil illumination. The five thousand who increased their arrogance have ceased from their seats;
Where can peach blossoms avoid the spring breeze?
Wandering through kalpas in solitude is truly pitiable; who would have known that the treasure-trove is naturally boundless? On the assembly at Vulture Peak, it was personally entrusted:
raising a hand or lowering the head—all is the separate transmission.
The Buddha’s entire body appears upon the tip of a hair; with every stroke and dot clearly defined, one beholds the pure cause.
Steadily riding the white ox toward the jewel-adorned destination, why linger further at the illusory city?
The Pure Land of Tranquil Light transcends past and present; the human world, like a dream or illusion, speaks of brevity and length. Once one realizes this sutra, there is no place to write it down;
without departing from the present thought, one beholds the King of Emptiness.
Six of Twelve Poems on Miscellaneous Scenes at West Lake:
Mr. Wang and Mr. Peng, these two rascals, chant "Buddha" in loud voices as they walk and then stop again and again.

Leisurely seeking the mountains above the lake, I sit and watch the waters below the peaks. What do the mountains and waters know? Yet lotus flowers grow from beneath my feet. Walking on, I ascend to Yunqi;
deep and secluded, an empty path opens before me. Unpacking my bundle, I lie upon the meditation couch, listening with clear ears to the sound of the spring.
Past and present are exactly thus. Show me the First Vehicle. Grasping my brush amidst the bamboo window, Master Hong acts as my witness.
From where did this peak (Feilai Peak) come? Where does it dwell now? Its dwelling place is utterly rootless; it is no different from its point of arrival.
As for its coming and going, from where do they ultimately proceed? It cuts off the path of thought; it is the boundless, eternally quiescent light. With whom can it be discussed?

Delusion and enlightenment lie between the southern path of the tomb-trees; Mount Yue’s grave towers over the northern lane. Two wells before the two graves share the name "Loyal Spring" (Zhongquan), their clarity and purity absolute.

A thousand frosts have washed the cold spirit; the cold spirit ascends to the midst of heaven. Vastly expansive, the lake's light is white; riding the clouds, it departs and returns once more. Do not—
Questioning the traces of rise and fall, the old man Wu of Xilin was skilled at explaining the meaning of *Vijñaptimātratā*; all quarters bowed their heads before him.

He received a prediction of future Buddhahood from Maitreya and made a vow to await his next life, resolving to complete the Great Matter through renunciation. If he intended to complete it, or has already completed it, why use further deliberation?
Whether lying down or rising, dwell in the Amitābha hermitage; proclaim the name of Amitābha Buddha. Amitābha neither comes nor goes; it is you yourself who are content with retreat and submission.

For the single thought-moment of an ordinary person, there is no need to beg from a Buddha. It is like holding a mirror to see one's own beard and eyebrows: within the mirror, there is fundamentally nothing [external] to be found.
When Master Xiangshan was about to pass away, a person asked:
"A hundred anxieties are empty; where in the realm of tranquil light (jìguāng) do east and west lie? Is it not a trivial matter for the Golden Terrace to lower its hand?
He smiled and pointed, saying: "The long wind carries the wild geese far."
With a mother’s urgent heart, words flow endlessly; Forfeiting my private kindness, two rows of tears fall. Having completed one hundred and eight verses of verse, the pure realm is opened;
The light pervades everywhere with the fragrance of white lotuses. (There are one hundred and eight poems on the Pure Land.)
The wind and moon over the Five Lakes remain as they were of old; throughout the long days in the mountains, I sleep soundly by myself. Having fished out all the golden-scaled fish, I have ceased;
my solitary thoughts rest beside the mattock.
The elders of the Dharma-gate are daily wasting away; I incline my ears to the once-struck notes of the vermilion strings. I pray you will leave behind for gods and men a standard of vision;
after adding incense to the burner, I urge you to take more nourishment.
Someone presented me with a newly carved edition of Xu Xiake’s *Travel Records* and I returned it with this poem:
"Whom do these green shoes and cloth socks hasten? They have trodden across the ends of the earth, their beards turned white by frost. I yield to you, Master, who have nothing to do;
With the day long, you rest on high pillows and commune with the Sage of Xihuang."
Two Verses on Uncle Sun Gongzhi’s Painting of *Cane-Wielding on an Autumn Mountain* The autumn mountain is also part of the human world;
One suffers as one goes back and forth within it. If you understand that Caoxi has not a single thing, Where in the human world can you seek an autumn mountain?
Autumn mountains are not of this human world; within the eternal light of *samantaprabhā*, coming and going are severed.
If you can realize that "the spring breeze is with me and Zhan," where in the human realm is there not an autumn mountain?
Inscribed for Jiang Sheng Zhao:
I once dreamed I was a kite, soaring high up to the Ninth Heaven; I also once dreamed I was a fish, diving deep down to the Ninth Abyss.
Who would have known that my original nature is neither fish nor kite? It is merely a chance transformation following external things, a shifting manifestation without beginning or end.
Upon waking, I wipe my eyes; heaven and abyss remain as they were. The countenance of Master Jiang within the painting exists amidst both certainty and doubt.
Wearing a tall cap, one enters the mundane world; baring the crown of the head, one flees to Chan. It is better to leave both aside and reflect back upon the state prior to birth.
What more could there be in that which has not yet arisen? A stone cauldron wafts clouds of tea smoke.
Among these ten verses on closing the gate, this is the fourth:
"At the gateway of merit and virtue, what is truly real? At one's feet, how many springs have been left in disarray? Now, I dedicate this toward the unborn."
In the kingdom, the butterfly frequently dozes within its meditation niche.
The True Body of our Buddha pervades the ten voids; in every atom, all is quiescent extinction with nothing remaining. Cease using knowledge and views to engage in further discrimination;
in a single thought, turn the light inward and recognize Him.
Dwelling deep within the garden, it is as silent as a mountain. Throughout the long day, who else would knock upon the gate? I inform you all: guard and cherish this place with diligence;
do not strive in vain to pursue it from outside the door.
Once again I turn toward Mount Ni to seek our old covenant; with a resonant *qin* lute, we speak of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Beneath the lotus feet, vast as a wheel, he strides through the spring wind of the Yi River with arms swinging free.
Jiang Jiuzhang of Baoshan purchased a residence at Nanyuan and took Su as a concubine. Su maintained a lifelong fast and honored the Buddha;

she moved to plant plum blossoms apart from her former grove. Beside the shrine of Prince Qi, she found solace in her secluded heart. Over a small bridge where the water flows, passersby [gaze upon] her scene.

Twilight. In ancient alleys and layered gates, fallen leaves lie deep. The wind stirs the Milky Way, evoking pity for Weaver Woman; incense lingers in the embroidered chambers, bringing to mind Avalokiteśvara.
At the stream before me, I stand listening as the fisherman’s song begins; one verse of the "Canglang" flows with a heart beyond this world.
At the Purple Bamboo Grove of Nanyuan, he established an image of Wenchang and instituted the Ceremony for the Veneration of Written Characters.
He inscribed the following on the ceremonial register: "Who will follow the Compassionate Vessel from the Southern Sea? A modest retreat at the city corner, where the bamboo paths are cool.
Having realized that the Golden Sutra is originally without characters, It emits auspicious light from within the flames of the red furnace."
Wenchang, the Lord of Destiny, crowns the Three Terraces; he once came from the West to bestow a prophecy. First, he broke down the barriers between Confucianism and Buddhism;
heaven and earth were overturned in a single furnace of ashes.
Ten Poems on Surveying Antiquity by Guan Ling Yinxī Who was that person beneath the pillar with whom I once traveled back and forth? Coming from the West, we met arm-in-arm and shared a smile.
Since the Blue Ox departed, there has been no news; I stand alone before the remaining books, growing old as a gatekeeper.
The madman of Chu, Jieyu, wanders among the tangled brambles; where does he wish to go? Gazing west toward Mount Qi, he dwells on his longings.
In sorrow the music ends and the man is gone; in the dream of the Duke of Zhou, his hair is already like silk.
Having received the teachings of the Magistrate of Lacquer Grove, my tongue repeatedly plays with the void. Who can fathom the beginning and end of this "suspended liberation"?
Leaning on my pillow, I briefly return to the dream of the Hu die; emperors, kings, and hegemonarchs are but a single tumbleweed drifting away.
The Fisherman of Jiang and Xiang: Intoxicated and sober, he transcends and attains freedom. His life’s journey is secure upon his simple skiff.
He leaves behind forever the waters of the Canglang River, Wherein the eternal sorrows of the Chu exiles are entirely extinguished.
The old man by the broken bridge came from nowhere and departed without cause; one might suspect he was the man who offered his shoes by the ford, yet again he bowed beneath Mount Gucheng.
Who would have known that he had already shed his mortal shell a thousand springs ago?
Liu Yimin: Beyond the kalpas, the lotus flower does not reckon spring. With a vow sworn to the mountains, one attains the ford for returning home.
Within the light of the white curl, there is no obstruction; how could even a single speck of dust ever settle upon one’s feet?
Master Fu: Returning from a lingering dream beneath the twin śāla trees, a flash of lightning illuminates the Tuṣita Palace.
Ultimately, humans and devas alike enter quiescent extinction; the perfect sound never ceases as it proclaims the Diamond Sūtra.
Han Shanzi: Serene and ethereal, he appears as a phantom among men; from the empty mountains, he sings out the sounds of antiquity.
Lü Qiu, burdened by many affairs, brought these points to light; thus, the pure breeze and bright moon endure unto this day.
Master Li: Boundless lands are not separated by the tip of a single hair; within the divine reliquary, the Dharma-realm is vast.
A single beam of white light frequently illuminates the night; even unto this day, the spring water has never run dry.
Master Pang: His livelihood of winnowing is chilled by the autumn wind; his children huddle together as the four walls stand empty.
Having drunk the Western River until not a single drop remains, there is no need to discuss wondrous functions or supernatural powers.
Two Poems Presented to the Venerable Weiran at Suyun Hermitage Braving the rain, I summoned you for a fine meeting;
mooring my boat, I visited the sick monk. The path is deep and the gate is silent; the mountain rises up as the thatched roof layers upon layers.
The shadow fades from the distant heavens like a crane; the light remains as the lamp of the ancient Buddha. Tranquil is the trace of one in the dust and market; once gone, fire melts the ice.
In the boundless ocean of the Flower Treasury, who can seek a ferryboat? A single drop flows from the faculty of the tongue; the palm leaves emit a wondrous radiance.
Relying on the supreme dedication, my autumn heart endures the evening cool. Do not let the six periods of the day pass in vain; the wind draws forth the fragrance of white lotuses.
Two Poems on Visiting Baiyun Spring and Ascending to the Summit of Tianping:
I have heard it said that in years of drought, this spring alone does not dry up. From where is its source known? Its reflection grows cold within these depths.
Observing the world, there is originally no trace; Incense burning, I attain still contemplation. Having finished drinking a cup of tea, I do not yet perceive the setting sun’s decline.
With staff in hand, I achieve this solitary appreciation; A precarious cliff pierced by a single thread. The path winds around the ridge of the hermitage; The rocks hang over the edge of the cottage.

At every step, one doubts there is no path; at every peak, it seems one is about to reach heaven. Where the pine wind passes slowly, the hundred-and-eight prayer beads are complete (at this time, sitting beneath a tree, chant the Buddha’s name a thousand times).
A monk from Lingyin Monastery presented me with fruits as large as apricots that were sweet in flavor. They grew on trees, yet had neither seeds nor pits, nor did they have flowers;
thus they were called "flowerless fruits" (wuhua guo). The monk said that these exist only within this monastery, and he too did not know from whence they originally came.
Standing alone as supreme beyond the catalog of myriad flowers, this pure land uniquely abounds in the grace of rain and dew.
There are many in the world—deceitful charlatans—who swallow everything at once, skin and marrow together.
In response to Wang Guanglu Mingsheng’s visit, following his rhyme:
The heart beneath the black gauze cap is one with the white gulls; The small boat drifts back and forth, west and then east. For twenty years, mist and clouds have lingered at the market of Meiwei;

For a thousand autumns, strings and pipes have resounded in the palace of King Lu. (Regarding the posthumous title of Guanglu as Minister Cheng) A connoisseur has the intent to seek the flowing water; To form—

For how many years have I bowed beneath your wind? In silence I sit, burning incense to pass the long day. Once again, with this bald brush, I offer a libation to the void, inscribing this "Diagram of the Three Teachings:
Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism. The Void speaks with a silver tongue; it paints shadows and figures, leaking forth the essence of spring. Who is the host? Who is the guest?
Blazing with discernment, I ask the "dumb sheep" for its response; like snow falling upon a red-hot furnace.
On New Year’s Eve, I boil tangerine cakes mixed with rock sugar as wine. This is presented on the occasion to honor Mr.
Qiushi.
A cup of crystal-clear broth, freshly infused with the fragrance of tangerines. It reaches the mouth but does not cause intoxication; pouring from the jar, it is an inexhaustible spring.
With this single lamp, we share this evening; seated side by side, we are two men at leisure. Waving away the affairs of the mundane world, we enter the dream-land of Huaxu again and again.
One of Two Poems on Recalling the Past at the Jade Altar:
At midnight, the sound of the bell tests my feathered robe; In the clouds, the gates of Changhe appear in a hazy dream. Now I turn my devotion toward the Land of Lotus Flowers;
The secluded Mount Penglai has its old doors closed.

Lu Langfu, having requested leave from his post as Provincial Governor of Shandong to return home and care for his mother, was presented with a painting of him visiting plum blossoms at Mount Dengwei as a parting gift.
He now brings it forth to request an inscription. His petition to serve his mother is most earnest;
A painting is newly rendered to express the sorrow of parting. The mountain peaks lie beyond the horizon on his oars; The lake’s radiance is springtime within his dreams.
The fragrance of the flowers is full and round; the spirit of the moon is elegant and detached. I intend to take up my staff and go forth to seek this incense at this very hour.
During the latter part of the second lunar month, I was joined by Mr. Wang Zidaishen, Mr. Lu Peiming, and Mr. Cheng Shairen.
I visited Master Sha Wengdouchu and proceeded to Shen’s Garden to view the peach blossoms;

revisiting old acquaintances, we spoke of the setting sun. Guided along winding paths and circling through long corridors, amidst the sparse and scattered trees in the spring breeze, one can truly exhaust the fragrance of the blossoms that fills the entire courtyard.
Old Man Zhu came to the courtyard; because he sought a preface for his *Baiyuan yeyu* (Hundred Cases of Karmic Retribution), I composed a poem and gave it to him.
I have long heard that Li Boshi was peerless in the world for painting horses, yet when he saw Chan Master He Xiu, the master told him he would surely fall into the belly of a horse.
Lu Zhi composes licentious verses; the retributions of hell are difficult to redeem. Saṃsāra has no fundamental root; a single thought serves as its hub.
Delusory thoughts bind together like flowers in the sky; they entangle one another in continuous succession. Lust truly governs the pivot; through this, one revolves and sinks into impurity.
Piteous are those like Xun and Pan; freshly adorned with moistened oils and balms (Pan Yue and Xun Can, who fell into female bodies as recorded in the *Zhishen lu*).

Their cosmetics soak their hollow entrails, while their whiskers and brows daily diminish. Their passions are vast, yet their spirit grows ever more subtle; they pursue one another like mandarin ducks. This principle is as clear as a painting; a thousand sages have successively expounded it.
To those who have realized the mind, right and wrong are as expansive and indifferent as deadly poison. From of old, this has been the ground upon which they dwell.

Fat! How could one possibly climb such divine feet? Having happened to let go on a precipice, once fallen, there is no returning. You, Master, possess a numinous root; your new verses are as elegant as orchids and chrysanthemums.
Through the conditions of this life, you have produced exquisite speech; your spring-like heart stirs amidst the green waters. Once the fragrance of flowers has passed, it does not remain;
those who see them are left with nothing but empty contact. Why not take up a single torch to sweep away the desires that scrape the heavens, and instead mount the Prajñā?
Light! Sitting, I inhale the fragrance of sandalwood; carving my heart, I aspire to the nine grades of rebirth. Waving my hand, I bid farewell to the five turbidities.
This humble person of dull faculties leans against a withered tree in a cold crag. Far distant are the traces left at Donglin; I long to bathe in the same waters of nourishment.
Though I lack the refined elegance of your writings, I offer this in modest imitation of the way one polishes jade.
A single branch of peony in the vase before the Buddha, a phantom sent with celestial fragrance;
within the deep waters of samādhi, the reflection of vows remains cool. I reckon there are but a few days left of the spring breeze;
it would be well to turn back from the dreams of the mundane toward the Empty King.
Passing beneath Lingyan Mountain, I recall the site of Tao Shi’s garden, where the Daoist Qiong-lou once read his books;
by the old traces on the stone piers, the winding path is now overgrown with fallen peach blossoms.
Wishing to inquire of my past three lives regarding cause and effect, a single bell tolls as the sun slants down upon the peak.
Presenting these Verses on Occasion at the Start of Summer to My Fellow Residents:
With carefree ease I bid farewell to spring; In leisurely verse I face the splendor of things. The duckweed parts as fish find rain; Branches stir as birds finish their blossoms.
Vegetables serve as the master’s meal; incense is shared with the monks’ tea. Do not sigh deeply over your羁愁 (traveler’s sorrows); within the three realms, there is no home at all.

On New Year’s Eve, I am moved by the neighbor’s rooster, which vyingly crows first night after night. Arriving here, I pass through the fifth watch in solitude. Blood stained by a thousand blades flows on—unending.
All is finished. With another cup of wine, we speak of the burgeoning spring.

Revisiting Shibi, I cherish this lake light that enters my gaze with its level serenity. As I sit, the weight of body and world becomes as light as a single hair. The old monk smiles and points toward the mountain’s visage.
Excellent. When facing others, how could one ever ask for their names?

The correspondence between Zhou Zhongjie and Wen Wensu—two mirrors reflecting each other’s light—is a single volume of writing where the sincere heart is laid bare with nothing further remaining; it is the ordinary practice of achieving righteousness and taking honor.
Matters: How could the fires at the end of the kalpa ever consume the vast void?
When Yu Wen-shu inscribed his composition on the "Treatise on Dwelling in the Two Forests," I followed its original rhyme.
Its expansive flow is like the sound of water; Zongzi understood its meaning. The spiritual resonance lies in the subtle and indistinct; how could it concern the affairs of the physical frame?

The great text originally has no text; returning to the root, they are fundamentally non-dual. Let us encourage one another through the cold of winter, withdrawing into seclusion to preserve our upright spirit.
The time will surely come when we reach the heavens; the role of beam and ridgepole is no small task.
In response to Li Luyi, I immediately sent this back to Jianning.
In years past, when I read the poems of the poets, I was particularly fond of those by Yuanming (Tao Qian) and also Taibai (Li Bai): "The idle clouds have no heart, drifting and never gathered;
the great Peng brushes the void—how can its traces be found? Later, I followed my teacher to the Anlewo (Anle Hut), where I drank wine beneath the plum blossoms and listened to his teachings.

A Pure Song: Later, I visited old friends on the path of Cold Mountain; ten-thousand-fathom clear pools reflect a single bright moon. The reflection of that single moon manifests in three thousand colors;
who can fathom its tranquil and profound true source? Carving ice and chiseling jade are but vain efforts.
I turn my merit toward Vimalakīrti’s single silence. Yesterday a guest called at my forest gate; his robes were elegant and he wafted the fragrance of orchids and herbs. He emerged from the stream...
My family collection has led me to read this; its appreciation, from morning till evening, is enough to make one forget hunger. He says of himself: "I once occupied the summit of a solitary peak;

having cleansed the spirit-mirror (lingtai), the night-light shone brightly. Yet the immortal plain was but a few inches away, and I became lost; at the river crossing, autumn deepens as severed twigs drift away."

The cry of the wild goose is urgent as I transcribe these remaining words; coolness arises in the courtyard trees, hastening the falling of shadows. In the blink of an eye, clear frost clings to my silvery hair;
dwelling in solitude and estrangement, I can only choke back my grief. I urge you, as you depart, not to linger long;
if one hears the Way at dawn, all affairs come to rest. Flowers bloom and fall without a master; do not vainly lament your parting sorrows to the spring breeze.
*Song of the Woodcutter’s Chant, Presented to the Wood-gatherer* (Luyizi Xianghu) The sound of hewing wood rings out as verse and response;
The preceding note has passed, the succeeding one hard to retain.
If you can grasp the true message from within this, It is neither Guo nor Huai—tranquil and beyond grasping.
In Response to Wang Nianfeng, the Second of Four Poems:
A single branch of plum buds heralds the early spring; Within the deep paper curtains, dreams are frequently pierced. Who would cast their gaze upon the flower before it blooms?
In the desolation of the frosty sky, its entire form is revealed.

Plucking strings and blowing bamboo pipes are at their finest; (Master Nianfeng once remarked that the brilliance of ice and snow brings forth the art of blowing bamboo and plucking strings. Moreover, there is a bright pearl whose price is beyond repayment.
It can sustain the inexhaustible offerings of devas and humans; where, then, could one find the leisure for sorrow while tending the lamp?
Two Poems on the Long-Vow Buddha-Stitching Society Recalling the sour and salty flavors of coarse grain and grass, I am reminded of my widowed state;
yet hearing the *Shao* music, how is it any different from sitting at the Zen barrier? Since time immemorial, the simple and pure has honored our Way;
there is no need to inquire about the asceticism of the Snowy Mountains.
Burning a pig—Master Foyin was being overly busy; it was simply because that bearded old man was a gourmand.
Having thoroughly cleansed the root of his tongue to restore its original state, this flavor belongs to us alone.

Epigraph for the Sixteen Poems on the Adornments of Sukhāvatī (The Rebirth of the Nine Grades) A single thought of sincere devotion brings one home early; Silently, one cuts off the myriad diverging paths. As wild geese fly across the vast sky, they leave no trace;
Yet with eyes closed, one vainly debates the red and white flowers.

(Three Sages’ Reception) To see the Buddha upon the blossoming of the flower is but ordinary; throughout the entire realm, all is luminously manifest, free from concealment. Do not speak of the ten trillion *yojanas* of distance;
where in the *śāntaprabhāsvara-loka* (World of Tranquil Light) could boundaries exist?
(The Water of the Pond of Merit): Its purity within admits nothing else; even a gentle breeze at the surface of the duckweed stirs ripples.
Each leaf and each flower is an inexhaustible treasury—how could one’s inspiration not flourish while sitting steadily here?
(Vairocana Jewel Ground) Once I beheld the great waters frozen into ice; a single flavor of cool clarity, utterly free from love and hate.
At dawn before the mirror, cease recognizing the reflection; throughout the entire teaching, there is ultimately nothing to rely upon.
(Seven layers of rows of trees) The rows of trees interlace their light, illuminating the water’s edge. Across the great trichiliocosm of sand-grain worlds, the barriers and ferries are cast open.
There is no need to distinguish between flowers and fruit; upon the shadowless branches, spring does not cling.
(Sevenfold Balustrades) The great gate of generosity stands open, free from self-interest; jeweled railings encircle it in shifting patterns.
Knowing that the scenery of the old garden remains unharmed, it would not be too late to return with sleeves brushed clean.
(Bathing in the Jewel Pond) I recall the ancient inscription on the bronze basin, ever-new in its lesson; The spring breeze of the Yi River path I have traversed once more.
Having begged for but a single spoonful of water from the Western Pond, Where could the lotus not stand tall and upright?
(Walking upon the Jewel Ground) Spring fills the eyes; the gates stand unbarred. Morning and night, all is vast and serene.
Even if one were to tread every path to the ends of the earth, one would not depart from this single bay of lotus-flowers.
(As for the Śrāvakas' further cultivation: How could the noble understanding sink into the ten stages of dhyāna? Hearing sounds and seeing forms, they transcend them all.
When spring arrives, the single rain makes no distinction; where among the mountain flowers would they not display their beauty?
(The Assembly of Supreme Goodness) The ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows fills the void; within it, the single path home is open.
If you do not understand the final verse of the Avataṃsaka, you will weep in your wretched plight amidst the autumn winds and rains.
(Heavenly Flowers Spread Upon the Ground) Pale red and deep purple reflect the morning mist; they fly on purpose to punctuate the void. Entirely elegant and flowing, they have no fixed abode;
they laugh at Śāriputra for being the only one whose robes were moistened.

(Heavenly music resounds in the void. When the wind ceases among the rows of trees, they no longer sound of their own accord; the void once again converses on non-arising. Who can truly comprehend this foremost of all-pervasive penetration?
Amidst the sounds of flutes and pipes, parting and welcoming are brought to an end.
(All the birds sing in harmony: In the third month, the southern garden’s foliage has turned deep green; From branches high and low, they send forth their melodious songs.
Severing the tongues of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions— The plucking of the flower and the smile remain even now.

(Offerings to the Ten Directions) With diligent devotion, a single thought encompasses all; Throughout the ten directions, where is there not this same flow? From the beginning, there has been no thread beneath one’s feet;
The bright moon and clear breeze are left to their own coming and going.
(Endless Towers and Pavilions) In the void there is a path, yet it is beyond all climbing; The layered towers and pavilions enter the gaze, causing one to lose their way.
If you can comprehend the inexhaustible meaning herein, Cease trying to contain the great ocean within the hoofprint of an ox.

(Within the boundless ocean assembly,) the ten-thousand-ri wide tides of the vast blue sea are sucked dry; golden-scaled fish, freed from the net, all enjoy carefree ease. Without leaving this very place, one hears it directly;
throughout every atom of the Dharma-realm, it vanishes in response to a single thought.
The Venerable Gaotang returned from Wutai Shan and was invited to reside at Haihui Hermitage. Two poems were composed as a substitute for a letter:
The path to Mount Tai is not far when traveling straight ahead; By chance, I shared a cup of tea with Wenxi. In the South, the Buddha-dharma is not much in abundance.
My son, with a single straw hat, the autumn wind reaches every home.
The gateways are desolate and the creeping weeds grow deep; do not allow worldly anxieties to intrude for even a moment.
The texts of Shimen and the verses of Hanshan—how can they be sought by writing them upon the void? Where would one find them?
Formerly, when the Venerable Wén asked the Daoist Zhīguī, "Since there is not an inch of soil upon the great earth, where can one find a place to settle the body and establish one's life?
The Daoist replied, "The sea is vast; let the fish leap as they will."
"Let birds fly freely across the sky. Master Wang Shikang painted his own portrait and requested that I, a monk, provide a phrase for it.
Finding myself with not a single tile above and not a needle’s point of ground below, I immediately recalled the previous conversation and appended this poem.
The vessel-world is utterly demolished, severing all causes and dependencies; it does not obstruct the soaring of the kite or the leaping of the fish.
If you can realize the intimate phrase within this, the hundred-and-eight beads of the rosary will exactly meet the occasion. (In the painting, he holds a rosary in his hand.)

Having read the various works of Wang Nianfeng, I have not yet severed the threads of emotional attachment that pursue form and fragrance; for three springs, my butterfly-dream has been frantic and wild. One must know that the present thought has no root or stem;
before the jade mirror stand, it has already begun to radiate light.
Inscription on the Portrait of Wang Lüzhai In years past, I hoisted my rush-sail and traveled far beyond ten thousand *li*. The palaces of white silver were close enough to reach;

purple shells and bright pearls were gathered as easily as picking mustard seeds. Returning, I settled by the banks of the Xu River. This coarse scholar, with his simple and meager fare, felt a particular kinship with you. At your study...
Flowers and medicinal herbs share words of empathy; before the gate, fish and birds frolic together in spring. (You are fond of releasing living beings. Last year I visited the path of Hanshan;
I personally reached Mount Tiantan to gather jade-like herbs. Carrying them back with sleeves full of white clouds, I entrusted them to Gantang Pavilion, where they remain untended.
My beard and brows appear as if depicted in a painting; my life and world have always been like duckweed upon the water. For your sake, I shall perform this one song.
Song of Non-Arising: The moon is at the edge of the sky, its reflection in the window-lattices.

*Short Verses on Land Travel* (Recorded as Four):
Since the time I first tied up my hair, I have crossed the Yellow River nine times. Looking at my reflection, I suddenly hesitate; in every new moment, there is no trace of the old steps.
Yesterday I dwelt in a magnificent hall; tonight I rest in a thatched cottage. Upon this single pillow, both master and servant have forgotten their cares.

Those who travel by water resent the heavens for the wind; those who travel by land resent the heavens for the rain. Yet what do the wind and rain know? It is but the human heart that harbors many obstructions.
Amidst the wind and sand during the day, I unexpectedly see a branch (there is a plum blossom in the guest house). Its character is cold and austere amidst the mountains;
do not let the people of the world know of it.
Ordinary, ordinary—sitting with my door closed. Stupefied, not a single word. Traveling on official duty is likewise incidental; The world rolls on, beyond my control.
Speech and silence are without intention, Just like painting withered branches. Yet suddenly spring comes to those withered branches, And the flocks of birds mingle their songs.
Irregular and uneven. When smelled, nothing at all is perceived; when touched, it is likewise unknown. At the very moment the brush first touches the paper, who ultimately presides over it?
Herein one must fix the eye with urgency; how could ten thousand transformations ever deceive?
This is the Gate of Non-duality, as taught by Vimalakīrti. Having received a letter from Wang Nianfeng, I remained dejected and unhappy for a long time. There was no end to it.

The vast sky holds not a drop of water; for whom does the thirsty deer toil in haste? One exerts oneself to vie for a place in the green annals; sad songs fill the brocade pouch.
The full moon is met by rain; the beautiful flowers do not withstand the frost. There is another recluse dwelling in seclusion, whose temple bell accompanies the setting sun.
With the monastic quarters closed for the retreat, I happened to examine a scroll of poems written in hand by Master Baisha, and have composed four verses in his rhyme.
I have just seen the plum branches blooming north of my inkstone; now I see the shadows of chrysanthemums reflecting east of my fence. To whom can I entrust the news within this realm?
An old fisherman by the river gate is left idly at leisure.
Once I held green silk reins as I traveled through remote frontiers; suddenly, this brief dream was shattered by the sound of bells. I laugh at Guan Zhong and Zhuge Liang—what did they accomplish?

The Lord of the Rushes takes up his brush, and dragons and snakes scurry; (the Master frequently uses rush pens. The *huantuo* dance flows with grace as the sleeves sway.

The cold permeates the solitary pavilion as the moon watches the fourth watch.
These waters and these mountains are all but dreams and illusions; neither mountain nor water, they are nonetheless expressed through words.
Now, having cut off both paths, the moon sets over the long river, yet remains ever full.

As I rise from illness, the cool air arrives before autumn; my single-layered robe feels light as I emerge from the bath. Deep within the curtains, flies keep their distance; as the flowers fade, the butterflies cease their pursuit.
I pity those in the burning house who share this same dream; I recall our old vow by the lotus pond. Having sat cross-legged upon the rope-cot for a long time, I idly stroll toward the bamboo grove.
In response to the original rhyme of Zhu Shijun’s gift:

Prosperity and decline have no inherent ground; stillness and resonance are one in the same sky. It is better to leave both aside and stretch out one’s legs to sleep by the south window.

Does the fisherman remember the path to the head of the creek? In silent solitude, the peach blossoms bloom for ten thousand ages of spring.
The Longjing bud tea is as subtle as the melodic resonance from Pengze’s zither;
its clarity rivals the poetic chants of Hanshan upon the rocks. A single cup dissolves away the long days amidst the pines and wind;
in this world, one may well find few who truly understand it.

Jiang Shantang lived in poverty yet maintained a rigorous resolve. His calligraphy was of exceptionally high caliber. Recently, he wrote for my son several chapters, including the *Paozang lun* (Treatise on the Treasure Store) by Master Zhaoming.

To see such a man upon these desolate rivers—remaining with the haughty bones of one who hung his door on a rope, with Buddhist scriptures as companions for his leisurely life—in the silent community of Donglin, let us hope to form a neighbor together.

Rolling up the painting and storing it on a high shelf, one sleeps with a pillow beneath the pines and the wind.
One of Two Poems Composed upon Returning Home from a Case of Shivering Fever:
My life of bowl and bamboo hat has wandered west and east; The green mountains are good companions, always in harmony.

The divine mechanism was once revealed to a monk in a dream; Half a verse was transmitted to illuminate the night lamp. Shake off your spirit and investigate the reality.
Phenomena arise like bubbles and vanish like bubbles; fundamentally, they have no basis.

What has been gained from this weary wandering? In a small pavilion, facing the green mountains. Pale blossoms break forth to welcome spring; A solitary staff accompanies the birds as they return.
Opening the volumes, I harbor thoughts of antiquity; peering into the mirror, I marvel at my new face. It is not that I have no acquaintances; I burn incense and love to close my door.

Cease being a guest at the ink-well; sit not idly waiting for your youthful countenance to wither.
In this small garden I pass the summer with miscellaneous verses;
the Qin steles and Han monuments are half-effaced by time. I feel weary as I laboriously wash my inkstone by the pond. I ask the void:
who has dipped his brush here? A single line of flying geese carries the returning clouds.
The medicine stove and tea mortar constitute my livelihood; wherever I happen to settle, it is as if I am being buried alive. All day long I sit with my head bared and go barefoot;
I have no further inclination to practice the "Heart-Sacrifice" (xīnzhāi).
The writings of Li Bai and Du Fu are but ashes from the kalpa’s end; the seasonal insects and birds needlessly suspect one another. In Vaiśālī, a single silence leaves nothing more to do;
it idly kills the few specks of moss before the steps.

Spending the year at Suimungsa Temple:

Chanting of the crickets as they groom their feathers for three autumn days, I long-sigh amidst the clusters of a hundred grasses. Relying on others ultimately leads to lost calculations; only by excelling on one's own does one truly claim the title of hero.
How could there be dreams of enfeoffment as a marquis? Who will pity the merit of successive battles? How much better it would be to escape the cage and go alone among the ten thousand mountains.
My nephew Xi-sou fell ill; reciting the Buddha’s name, he passed away. I compose this poem to bid him farewell:
Lotus flowers cover the entire world, their fragrance filling the nostrils. With a serene air, he has cast off his hands and returned home. Even Māra of Changli did not know the Western Land.

Ti. Awakened from her midnight slumber in the inner chambers (she had been suffering from abdominal tumors; while reciting the Great Compassion Mantra, she dreamed of an old woman who gave her a single flower branch, whereupon she suddenly felt her body as light as a feather and recovered quickly).
Appearing and disappearing in Jambudvīpa, you delude yourself with suffering; how many times have the waves of the river of craving ever dried?
